blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an m × n matrix, return all of its elements in **spiral order**: along the top row left to right, down the right column, back along the bottom row right to left, up the left column — then inward, and repeat.

blocks.alt: A 3 by 4 matrix with arrows tracing the spiral: 1, 2, 3, 4, then down to 8 and 12, back along 11, 10, 9, up to 5, then inward to 6 and 7. The outer ring is yellow and the inner ring blue.

blocks.text: A spiral is a series of **rings**, from the outside in. Each ring is four straight walks: one along each edge. The tricky part isn't the walking — it's knowing where each walk starts and stops, and not visiting a cell twice when the matrix isn't square.
The key insight: four shrinking boundaries
Track the part of the matrix you haven't visited yet with four variables: `top`, `bottom`, `left` and `right`. Walk one edge, then pull that boundary inward. Stop as soon as the boundaries cross.

blocks.alt: Four boundaries around the unvisited region. After walking the top row, top moves down by one. After the right column, right moves left. After the bottom row, bottom moves up. After the left column, left moves right.

items: Walk the **top** row from `left` to `right`, then `top++`.
Walk the **right** column from `top` to `bottom`, then `right--`.
If rows remain (`top <= bottom`), walk the **bottom** row from `right` to `left`, then `bottom--`.
If columns remain (`left <= right`), walk the **left** column from `bottom` to `top`, then `left++`.

blocks.text: Why the last two walks need an extra check

The boundaries move **during** one lap. Take a single-row matrix `[[1, 2, 3]]`: the first walk consumes the row and moves `top` past `bottom`. Without the `top <= bottom` check, the bottom-row walk would run over the same row again, duplicating every value.
The first two walks don't need a check, because the `while` condition was just confirmed. After `top++` and `right--`, it may no longer hold — so it has to be checked again.
The faded cells are outside the boundaries. Try a single row, a single column, and a 4 × 4 square.

blocks.alt: Spiral order: O(rows × cols) time and O(1) extra space besides the result.

blocks.text: Every cell is added exactly once: **O(rows × cols) time**, and only four boundary variables besides the output: **O(1) extra space**. (Another common solution walks with direction vectors and marks cells as visited — just as fast, but it needs an extra visited grid.)

items: **Square with an odd size** — the last ring is a single cell in the middle.

blocks.text: Where this idea shows up again

Shrinking boundaries handle any ring-by-ring processing: generating a spiral matrix from the numbers 1 to n², rotating each ring of a matrix, or printing a matrix in layers. The same four variables also describe the search space in some 2D binary-search problems.
